module_title: Expansion of British Power - Punjab, Sindh Annexation and Foreign Policies
introduction: This advanced level analyzes the British foreign policies aimed at securing the North-Western frontiers (Punjab, Sindh, Afghanistan), the diplomatic balancing act of Maharaja Ranjit Singh, the Anglo-Sikh Wars, and the highly controversial annexation of Awadh.

core_concepts.title: Annexation of Sindh (1843)
core_concepts.description: Following the disastrous First Afghan War, the British laid false charges against the 'Amirs' of Sindh. Led by Charles Napier, they annexed Sindh into the British Empire. It was widely seen as an immoral imperialistic move.

core_concepts.title: Anglo-Sikh Wars (1845-1849)
core_concepts.description: After the death of Maharaja Ranjit Singh (1839), Punjab descended into anarchy. Two Anglo-Sikh Wars were fought. After the Second War (under Lord Dalhousie) in 1849, Punjab was fully annexed, and the 'Kohinoor' diamond was taken from Maharaja Duleep Singh.

core_concepts.title: Annexation of Awadh (1856)
core_concepts.description: Lord Dalhousie annexed Awadh (an old and loyal ally of the British) based on James Outram's report alleging 'Misgovernance'. This deeply angered the sepoys and became a major cause of the 1857 Revolt.

core_concepts.title: Anglo-Nepalese War (1814-1816)
core_concepts.description: Fought between the Gurkhas and the British (Lord Hastings). It ended with the 'Treaty of Sagauli' (1816), granting the British hill stations like Shimla, Mussoorie, and Nainital.

core_concepts.title: British Afghan Policies
core_concepts.description: Fearing a Russian invasion, the British frequently changed their Afghan policies: ranging from Lord Auckland's aggressive 'Forward Policy' to John Lawrence's policy of 'Masterly Inactivity' (non-interference).

important_entities.name: Maharaja Ranjit Singh
important_entities.significance: He signed the 'Treaty of Amritsar' in 1809 with the British (Charles Metcalfe), accepting the Sutlej river as the boundary and maintaining diplomatic peace during his lifetime.

important_entities.name: Charles Napier
important_entities.significance: Regarding the annexation of Sindh, his famous (alleged) quote was: 'We have no right to seize Sind, yet we shall do so, and a very advantageous, useful, humane piece of rascality it will be' (Peccavi).

important_entities.name: Wajid Ali Shah
important_entities.significance: He was deposed on charges of misgovernance and exiled to Calcutta, which led to immense resentment among the public of Awadh.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.alert_title: Awadh wasn't annexed under the Doctrine of Lapse
trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: A very common mistake: Students assume Dalhousie annexed Awadh using the 'Doctrine of Lapse' (denial of an adopted son). No, Awadh was uniquely annexed on charges of 'Misgovernance' (Maladministration).

They are different individuals. Warren Hastings was the first Governor-General of Bengal (1773), whereas Lord Hastings (1813-1823) suppressed the Pindaris and completely destroyed the Maratha confederacy.

mnemonics_and_tricks.trick_title: Chronology of Doctrine of Lapse Annexations
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Satara (1848), Jaitpur, Sambalpur, Baghat, Udaipur, Jhansi (1853), Nagpur (1854).

exam_strategy_tips: Arranging the states annexed under the 'Doctrine of Lapse' in chronological order is a favorite question in UPSC and State PCS exams.
Pay special attention to the parties involved in the 'Treaty of Sagauli' (British and Gurkhas) and the year of the 'Treaty of Amritsar' (1809).
